In 1920, Edwin Hubble discovered that some of the diffuse patches observed with telescopes, which everyone thought were clouds inside the Milky Way, were in fact other galaxies. The application of the Doppler effect allowed him to observe that the galaxies were receding from one another and that, the farther away a galaxy was, the faster it receded. He concluded that this made it possible to find the distance to a galaxy from the famous equation:
$$\frac{\lambda - \lambda_0}{\lambda_0} = \left(\frac{H}{c}\right) r$$

where the value of $H$ is $\sim 77$ km/s/Mpc, $r$ is the distance measured in parsecs and $c$ is the speed of light. The term on the left is known as the redshift ($z$) and is determined by the displacement of the line analysed.

a) To which colour does the spectrum of a galaxy that is receding from the observer shift?

b) A galaxy has been observed to undergo a redshift of $z = 0.77$. Determine the distance at which this galaxy is located.

Today we know more than 250 stars that have planets. Indirect methods such as the "transit method" are the most efficient means of detecting and characterising extrasolar planets. The transit method can be used to detect planets if the star, the planet and the observer are aligned. What is done is to observe the light curve of the star and, from it, infer some information about the planets and their orbits. Assuming a circular orbit for the planet, the geometry of the transit can be described in a simple way by the following figure (Figure 1. Transit geometry).

In figure 1, "b" is the impact parameter (dimensionless), that is, the projection of the smallest distance from the centre of the planet to the equator of the star; "R" is the radius of the star, "a" is the orbital radius and "i" is the inclination of the orbit with respect to our line of sight. The duration of the transit is expressed as:
$$d \approx \frac{PR}{\pi a}\sqrt{\left(1+\frac{r}{R}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{a}{R}\cos i\right)^2} \qquad (1)$$

where r is the radius of the planet and P is the orbital period. In addition, the duration of the transit time "t" can be calculated by the equation:
$$t \approx d\,\frac{r}{R}\sqrt{1-b^2} \qquad (2)$$

The planet around the star HD 209458 was one of the first extrasolar planets detected by photometric methods. Using a 14" telescope the following light curve was obtained for HD 209458 (Figure 2. In the 1680s the Englishman Isaac Newton (1642–1727) proposed, to explain the theory of gravitation, that when launched from a cannon, positioned horizontally on the top of a very high mountain (to avoid friction with the atmosphere), at an appropriate speed (see Figure 1), a body would revolve forever around the Earth just as the Moon does. The idea of artificial satellites had been launched. Satellites are launched into space by rockets, which rise vertically and are gradually manoeuvred to acquire the horizontal orientation, as in the cannon of Figure 1. The Soviets were the first to achieve this feat, putting Sputnik into orbit around the Earth on 4 October 1957.

The Brazilian Space Programme is developing the Satellite Launch Vehicle (VLS), through the Institute of Aeronautics and Space (IAE), located in São José dos Campos, SP. To put a satellite into an orbit located 750 km from the surface of the Earth, it is necessary to reach a speed of 27000 kilometres per hour (parallel to the surface). Instead of the top of a mountain, the VLS is launched from the Alcântara Launch Centre (CLA), located on the coast of the northeast of Brazil at $2^\circ$ S latitude, see Figure 2.

To reach the speed of 27000 km/h, the VLS uses a large quantity of fuel (called propellant) which is distributed in seven motors, distributed in turn in four stages. The 1st stage consists of 4 motors. They are attached laterally to the central body composed of the 2nd, 3rd and 4th stages and the satellite, which is at the top of the rocket, protected by a cover called the fairing. The motors are burned successively and are discarded into the sea after the fuel has been consumed. As the launch takes place vertically, a series of events occurs in placing the satellite in orbit (Figure 3).

The propulsive force needed to launch the VLS (Satellite Launch Vehicle) from the ground, generated by burning the propellant of the four motors of the first stage, must be greater than the weight. In general, 80% of the fuel is consumed to overcome gravity and accelerate the rocket. The other 20% is consumed to overcome the drag force which results predominantly from the friction of the rocket with the atmospheric air.

The following table presents some events relating to the flight of the VLS, to place an 86 kg satellite in orbit. When activated, the four motors of the first stage of the VLS provide 1000000 N (one million) of thrust. The ignition of the second stage occurs 15 seconds before the end of burning of the four propulsors of the first stage, while the ignition of the third stage takes place only after the total consumption of the fuel of the second-stage motor.

Since above 100 km of altitude there is already the vacuum of space, the fairing that protects the satellite from atmospheric friction can be ejected; this happens 133 seconds into the flight. After the separation of the third stage, the fourth stage plus satellite assembly is inclined at $52^\circ$ with respect to the vertical. However, the ignition of the fourth-stage motor occurs only after a manoeuvre (tilting) whose function is to place the satellite/stage-4 assembly parallel to the Earth's surface, similar to the cannon of figure 1. The 36 seconds of burning of the fourth-stage motor are enough to reach the orbital speed of 7500 m/s. At the end of the total burning of the fuel of the fourth stage, it separates from the satellite and both remain in orbit around the Earth.

Problem 3. Earth–Sun thermal equilibrium

The Stefan–Boltzmann law states that a body emits energy per unit area per unit time in proportion to the fourth power of its absolute temperature, whose expression is $F = \sigma T^4$, where $F$ is the flux (power per area) and $\sigma$ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant. The power radiated (luminosity) by the Sun is:
$$P_S = \sigma\left(4\pi R_S^2\right)T_S^4$$

The Earth is continuously receiving the radiant energy coming from the Sun. At the same time the Earth as a whole radiates energy into space in such a way that it establishes an average temperature that is in equilibrium with the solar radiation. Find the expression for this average temperature of the Earth, knowing that the temperature of the solar surface is $T_S$, the terrestrial radius $R_T$, the radius of the Sun $R_S$ and the Earth–Sun distance $R_{T-S}$.

Question 8) The speed needed to put a rocket into orbit is 28 000 km/h. In most cases, the same rocket uses solid and liquid fuel. In space terminology, the fuel and the oxidiser are called propellants. In practice, the tonnes of propellant used to put a satellite into orbit are stored in different tanks, called stages. Thus, after the fuel of the first stage has been burnt, the fuel and oxidiser tanks are discarded and the flight continues, with successive activation of the other stages. Storing and carrying all the fuel and oxidiser in a single tank is inefficient, since during a good part of the flight it would be accelerating an inert mass, represented by the structure of the empty part of the tank. In general, the number of stages in a rocket varies between 3 and 4, since a larger number of stages requires additional mass to house the stage separation system.

The following table gives the velocity gain obtained by burning each of the four stages of the Brazilian Satellite Launch Vehicle (VLS-1) to launch a 100 kg satellite.

i) the ratio between the mass of the propellant and the total mass of the rocket at the moment of lift-off

ii) the ratio between the mass of the satellite and the total mass of the rocket at the moment of lift-off.

NOTE: Express your results as percentages.

The bodies of the Solar System are distinguished from other stars in several ways. In general, they have no internal sources of energy, and are detectable only through the solar radiation that they reflect or re-emit thermally. One consequence of this fact is that the energy coming from the Sun is also largely responsible for the temperatures of these bodies. For bodies without an atmosphere and without internal sources of heat, the highest possible temperature is obtained by assuming radiative balance between the surface of the body and the incident solar radiation. If we assume that there is no conduction of heat into the interior of the body, we have:
$$\varepsilon\,\sigma T_{SS}^4 = \frac{S_\odot}{R^2}(1-A)$$

In this equation we have:

• $T_{SS}$: subsolar point temperature, the point of the surface of the body that would be intercepted by an imaginary line connecting the centre of the body with the centre of the Sun;

• $\sigma$: Stefan–Boltzmann constant;

• $\varepsilon$: emissivity, which is the fraction of thermal radiation that the body actually emits and depends (weakly) on its composition. For an ideal emitting body, called a "black body", we would have $\varepsilon = 1$; values of $\varepsilon \approx 0.9$ are generally a good approximation for the bodies of the Solar System;

• $S_\odot$: solar constant, which is the total amount of energy emitted by the whole surface of the Sun in one second;

• $R$: the distance between the body and the Sun; and

• $A$: the hemispherical albedo of the body, which measures the fraction of the incident energy that is reflected by the body and depends on its composition.

With this, the equation states that the amount of thermal energy emitted in one second per unit area of the body ($\varepsilon\sigma T_{SS}^4$) at a given point of its surface must be equal to the amount of energy per unit area incident on that point $\left(\dfrac{S_\odot}{R^2}\right)$ and absorbed by it $(1-A)$. 2) Space weather

Coronal mass ejections, CME (Coronal Mass Ejection), are large eruptions of high-temperature ionised gas from the solar corona. The expelled gas becomes part of the solar wind and, when it reaches the Earth's magnetic field, it can cause storms, damaging communications and power stations. When an ejection is directed straight towards the Earth, the shock wave of the energetic solar particles causes a geomagnetic storm that disrupts the Earth's magnetosphere, compressing its field lines on the side facing the Sun and expanding them on the other side, producing a magnetic tail. When the magnetosphere reconnects in its expanded region, it releases energy on the terawatt scale, which is directed straight at the upper layers of the atmosphere. The solar energetic particles also cause polar aurorae in regions near the magnetic poles of the Earth. Geomagnetic storms can interrupt radio transmissions and can damage satellites and power stations, possibly causing blackouts.

In 2004, a team of North American astronomers observed the relation between the amplitude of the disturbance $P$, in nanotesla [nT], produced by the CME, and the magnitude of the component of the terrestrial magnetic field $B_z$, in nanotesla [nT], perpendicular to the plane of the Solar System at the time of the storm. The authors expressed this relation using the following formula (Yurchyshyn et al, 2004):
$$(1)\quad P = -2.846 + 6.54\,B_z - 0.118\,B_z^2 - 0.002\,B_z^3$$

Also in 2004, a team of Brazilian astronomers determined a relation between the propagation speed of the CME, $V$ in km/s, and the magnitude of the disturbance $P$, again in nanotesla [nT]:

Question 1: orbits of the planets

Determining the period of a planet requires some care, since the Earth, from where we make the observations, performs several motions depending on the reference frame adopted. We call the sidereal period ($P$) of a planet the time interval it takes to complete one orbit around the Sun. Question 3: Motion of the stars

Stars can move through space in any direction. The true velocity of a star describes how fast and in what direction it moves. As the following figure shows, the true velocity ($v$) of a star can be divided into two perpendicular components. One of them is the tangential velocity ($v_t$), perpendicular to our line of sight. To determine it, astronomers must know the distance ($d$) to the star and also its proper motion ($\mu$). Taking $\mu$ in seconds of arc per year and $d$ in parsecs, the value of the tangential velocity, in km/s, is determined by the relation:
$$v_t = 4.74\cdot\mu\cdot d$$

The component of the motion of the star parallel to our line of sight is called the radial velocity ($v_r$). Its value can be determined from the Doppler effect of the spectral lines of the star. If a star approaches, the wavelengths of its spectral lines decrease (blueshift). When the star recedes, the wavelengths increase (redshift).

Question 4: Hubble's Law

Suppose that you have a telescope at an observatory and you take the spectrum of a distant galaxy. When you examine it, you find that the spectral lines are shifted towards the red of the spectrum. The redshift of the galaxy ($z$) is given by:
$$z = \frac{\lambda - \lambda_0}{\lambda_0}$$

From the redshift we can determine the radial velocity of a galaxy, known as the recession velocity. If the redshift is less than 0.1, we can neglect relativistic effects, so that $v = c\cdot z$, where $c = 3\times10^{5}$ km/s is the speed of light.

As shown alongside [Graph 1], the relation between $z$ and $v$ is not always linear. If the redshift is greater than 0.1, then we must use the following relation:
$$v = \left[\frac{(z+1)^2 - 1}{(z+1)^2 + 1}\right]\cdot c$$

Knowing the recession velocity of the galaxy, we can determine its distance ($D$) from Hubble's Law:
$$v = H_0\cdot D$$
where $H_0 = 73$ km/s/Mpc is the Hubble constant.
